analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal insurance program paying workers up to three months of partial wages for family or medical leave.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee: it was introduced in February 2017 with 36 Democratic and independent backers and received no hearing, no vote, and no action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The FAMILY Act would have given every working person in America paid leave — partial wage replacement — for up to 60 days when they have a baby, adopt a child, care for a seriously ill spouse, parent, or child, or deal with their own serious illness. It would have been run through the Social Security Administration and paid for by a new small payroll tax: 0.2% taken from both workers' paychecks and employers' payrolls, and 0.4% for the self-employed. Employers would also have been barred from firing or penalizing anyone who used the benefit. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers without paid leave through their employer. When the bill was introduced, only about 14% of U.S. workers had access to paid family leave, and just 4% of those in the lowest-paying jobs did. Nearly half of workers who qualified for unpaid federal leave reported they couldn't afford to take it. Benefits would have replaced roughly a share of the worker's highest recent year of income, between a floor of $580 and a cap of $4,000 per month, prorated for the days of care actually taken.

how_it_helps.text: Every worker insured under Social Security who has recent earned income would be entitled to benefit payments for up to 60 caregiving days per benefit period, covering birth or adoption, a serious health condition of their own, or care for a child, spouse (including domestic partner), or parent with a serious health condition.

Benefits replace a portion of the worker's highest-earning recent year — the lesser of one-eighteenth of that year's income or $4,000 per month, with a floor of $580 — so part-time and low-wage workers get a meaningful payment rather than nothing.
Employers would be prohibited from firing or discriminating against a worker for applying for or receiving benefits, with workers able to sue for lost wages, reinstatement, and attorney's fees.

The program is paid for by a dedicated 0.2% payroll tax on both employees and employers (0.4% for self-employment income) flowing into its own trust fund, explicitly separate from the Social Security trust funds.

analysis.who_pays: Every employer and every employee would pay a new 0.2% payroll tax on all wages — about $100 a year for someone earning $50,000 — and the self-employed would pay 0.4%. Workers who never take leave would pay into the fund for others' benefit, which is how all social insurance works. Employers would also bear the cost of adjusting to a benefit their workers could claim regardless of company policy.
analysis.who_pays_short: All employers and workers via payroll tax

drawbacks.text: The bill taxes every worker and every employer 0.2% of wages (0.4% for the self-employed) whether or not they ever use the benefit, which opponents would call a permanent new tax during a period of unified Republican control focused on cutting taxes.

Benefits are limited to 60 caregiving days with a five-day unpaid waiting period, and the monthly amount is prorated by days of care taken, so workers needing intermittent or partial leave receive reduced payments.

A universal public benefit would partially substitute for private short-term disability and paid-leave products that employers already buy, and employers — even those sympathetic to paid leave — would lose control over how leave is provided at their firms.

Critics of a federal social-insurance approach have generally preferred voluntary or employer-based alternatives, such as letting new parents draw down their own Social Security benefits early, arguing a mandate is the wrong model.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is broad and concrete: paid leave for a life event almost every worker eventually faces, with the largest gains going to low-wage workers, who today almost never have it. The cost side is real but modest and broadly shared — roughly $2 a week for a worker earning $50,000, matched by the employer. The bill is relatively well designed for honesty: it funds itself through a dedicated tax and trust fund rather than borrowing. The main design limits are the 60-day cap and the waiting period. The unresolved question is the tax's weight on employers who already offer generous leave, which is why business groups typically prefer tax credits for voluntary arrangements.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Finance Committee for the rest of the 115th Congress — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and died when the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the FAMILY Act on February 7, 2017, joined by 27 original Senate cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day; that referral is the last entry in its action history.
The bill had 34 cosponsors in total — 32 Democrats and 2 independents — with no Republican support.
The Senate Finance Committee, chaired by a Republican, never took the bill up, and it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have paid the new 0.2% payroll tax, and opponents of expanding federal social insurance, are better off because the bill died without a vote. Workers without employer-paid leave gained nothing, and continue to rely on whatever their employer offers.

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the FAMILY Act and was its lead sponsor.

for.name: 32 of 46 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it the support of most of the Senate Democratic caucus.

against.name: Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill's action history ends with the referral.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor in the two years it sat in committee.

against.name: Employer and business associations
against.what_they_did: Generally opposed mandated payroll-tax-funded paid leave, favoring voluntary employer arrangements instead.

sides.party_line_note: All 36 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or independents; no Republican backed it, and the Republican-controlled Finance Committee took no action on it.

industries.note: Every employer would pay a new 0.2% payroll tax and lose discretion over leave policy. The bill's own findings cite California data showing most employers rated a similar state program positive or neutral for their business.

industries.industry: Short-term disability and paid-leave insurance providers
industries.note: A public benefit covering the same life events would substitute for the employer-provided disability insurance that fewer than 40% of workers have today, shrinking the market for private plans. Private plans profit by restricting access; a public program that pays directly competes with that.
